nodes.label: Truncation-Artifact Flagging Mechanism
nodes.rationale: A truncation cutoff landing extremely close to (but not on) an existing vertex ring can produce near-zero-length chords or near-zero-area panels. Rather than silently including or dropping these, any chord/panel under 0.1% of the dome's largest strut length is surfaced in a dedicated 'Possible truncation-artifact' list so builders don't have to eyeball a long report.

nodes.label: Rotation-Invariant Hub Template Clustering
nodes.rationale: Hubs are clustered by a rotation-invariant shape signature (valence + cyclic pattern of angular gaps/tangential angles) at 3-decimal precision. This precision was tuned empirically because the geometry pipeline's floating-point noise reaches the 6th decimal place, and using 6-decimal precision failed to merge otherwise-identical hubs, silently doubling the reported template count.

nodes.label: Python 2 to Python 3 Port
nodes.rationale: Codebase was ported from Python 2 to 3; most Py2-isms (bare except:, wildcard imports, deprecated numpy.linalg.linalg/numpy.matrix API, 1-indexed vertex numbering) were cleaned up. Remaining unusual patterns (e.g. manual dict-based grouping in bill_of_materials.py instead of collections.defaultdict) are likely leftover holdovers, not intentional design.

nodes.label: pylair/class_three.py
nodes.rationale: A first per-face-independent implementation (merging only by 3D proximity, like Class I/II) satisfied Euler's formula and even the golden-value counts while still being wrong: it left all 30 original icosahedron edges unsubdivided, because a chiral (m != n) lattice has no reflection symmetry, so a point near a face's edge doesn't generally land at the same 3D position when computed independently by the neighboring face. The fix stitches adjacent faces together combinatorially, matching grid points by an integer index derived from the lattice's own structure rather than 3D coordinates, and was verified against antitile to within 1e-15 on the sorted, mean-normalized edge-length distribution.

nodes.label: pylair/bill_of_materials.py
nodes.rationale: -b/--bom-rounding controls both display precision and merge granularity: chords are grouped into BOM rows by clustering lengths (not independently rounding each) to avoid splitting one true strut length into multiple rows due to floating-point noise. Default 9 stays exact at any practical frequency; lowering it intentionally merges close-but-not-identical lengths for coarse fabrication tools, at the risk of merging lengths meant to be different.

nodes.label: Elliptical Stretching / Ellipsoid Elongation
nodes.rationale: Every downstream angle calculation (hub deflection, spoke, panel bevel) must use the true surface normal of the resulting general triaxial ellipsoid (the gradient of the ellipsoid equation) rather than the sphere's simpler radial-vector normal, which is only exact for a true sphere; this was double-checked against an independent numerical approximation of the same gradient before trusting it on more than one axis at a time.

nodes.label: Next Step: Unstrutted Diagonal / Quad Panel Handling
nodes.rationale: Clipping two or more axes through the same original triangle silently splits one physical quad panel into two unconnected triangles in the report. Proposed fixes: let a panel genuinely be a quadrilateral (big change, since SSS panel-type grouping and DXF templates assume triangles), or offer to add a real diagonal support strut across the seam.
nodes.norm_label: next step: unstrutted diagonal / quad panel handling

nodes.label: Next Step: Proactive Truncation-Risk Warning
nodes.rationale: A risky truncation cutoff producing absurdly small struts/panels is currently flagged only after the fact, buried in the BOM's artifact lists. A more proactive version would catch such cases before export and warn or refuse at the moment a chosen -t/-x/-y value lands suspiciously close to an existing vertex.

nodes.label: Next Step: Optional Boundary Capping
nodes.rationale: Truncation currently always leaves the cut boundary open (no floor/wall), correct for a dome sitting on the ground but not for a fully enclosed structure. An optional cap triangulating the boundary ring into real panels would suit enclosed-structure use cases.

nodes.label: AI-Assisted Development of pyLair (Claude Code collaboration)
nodes.rationale: Original pyLair implementation was written from scratch in Python by the author, then Claude Code refactored it to be PyPI-ready, and was subsequently used to collaboratively add Class II/III subdivision, sphere elongation, STL/OBJ/PNG output, face truncation, multi-axis ellipsoid projection, multi-axis truncation, and face-aware truncation. The blog post itself was ~95% manually written, with small outline assistance from Claude Code.
